title: MobileIPL: Teaching Mobile Agents to Think Better
one_liner: Score the final action, then trace backward through the reasoning tree to score each intermediate thought, and use those scores to train better reasoning.
lead: Mobile agents that look at phone screens need to explain their reasoning step by step. The problem: they lack diverse examples of good reasoning, and even with more training data, it is hard to know which intermediate thinking steps actually matter. MobileIPL solves this by scoring the final action, then propagating that score backward through the reasoning tree to label each intermediate thought with a value, creating a training signal that teaches the agent which reasoning paths lead to success.

paras: Mobile agents that interact with phone screens need to think through their actions step by step: look at the screen, decide what the goal is, figure out what button to press. The agent learns from examples of successful actions, but there is a catch: training data is scarce and expensive to collect. A beginner might try to just show the agent more examples of good actions, but this does not work well because the agent does not learn to think the same way humans do. It memorizes actions instead of developing reasoning steps.

The real problem is worse: even with more examples, nobody tells the agent which intermediate thinking steps were correct. The agent might think Step A, then Step B, then press Button C. Button C was right, but was Step B actually helpful? Was Step A clear? Without this fine-grained feedback, the agent treats all reasoning steps as equally valuable and does not improve its thinking, because during training it has no signal to distinguish which steps contributed to the success versus which were noise.

callout.html: Score the final action, then trace that score backward through the reasoning tree so that each intermediate step knows whether it helped or hurt.

panels.title: 1. The mobile agent sees a screen
panels.caption: Agent reads the screen image and starts reasoning about the goal.

panels.title: 2. It generates a tree of possible reasoning paths
panels.viz_args: Thought A → Thought B → Action (right), Thought A → Thought B' → Action (wrong), Thought A' → Thought C → Action (right)
panels.caption: Each sampled path explores different reasoning steps, all ending in actions.

panels.title: 3. Score the final actions against ground truth
panels.caption: The paths that pressed the correct button score high; wrong ones score low.

panels.title: 4. Backpropagate value to intermediate thoughts
panels.caption: Each thought gets a value score based on what actions it led to.

panels.title: 5. Train on the difference between good and bad reasoning
panels.caption: The agent learns to prefer high-value reasoning paths over low-value ones.

steps.text: For each goal, sample multiple complete reasoning trajectories (each reasoning step leading to an action sequence).
For each final action, check if it is correct; assign a reward: high for right actions, low for wrong ones.
Compute each intermediate reasoning step's value by averaging the values of the actions it led to.
Create preference pairs: a high-value reasoning path vs. a low-value one, both leading from the same earlier step.
Update the agent to prefer high-value reasoning over low-value reasoning using these preference pairs.

paras: MobileIPL does not change which buttons the agent presses. It changes the reasoning steps—the intermediate thoughts the agent generates before it acts. By scoring and training on these intermediate thoughts, the agent learns to think more like a human, not just guess the right action.

hidden.h2: The step value: which intermediate thoughts matter
hidden.name: Step value (the contribution of each reasoning step)
paras: The paper measures something that was never explicitly named before: the value of each intermediate reasoning step. A valuable step is one that, when included in a reasoning tree, consistently leads to correct actions, because that step filtered out bad directions or clarified the goal in a way the subsequent steps could build on. A low-value step does the opposite, either confusing later steps or pointing them toward wrong answers. By computing this value for every intermediate thought, the agent can learn which reasoning patterns work.

MobileIPL estimates step value by averaging the outcomes of all reasoning trees that included that step. If a step appeared in five different paths and four of them succeeded, that step gets a higher value than a step that appeared in paths with a 2/5 success rate. The paper then propagates this value backward through the tree using a simple average rule, treating earlier steps as contributions to their descendants.

heat.caption: Darker means higher step value (stronger predictors of correct actions). Highlighted thoughts led to the goal.

reads.html: Step value is how much a particular reasoning thought contributes to getting the final action right. High-value thoughts are the clear, honest reasoning steps that lead to correct button presses.

The paper computes step value recursively: the value of a leaf node is the reward of the action it produces (correct vs. incorrect); the value of an earlier step is the average of all its child nodes values, scaled by a discount factor.

mechanism.h2: Why the method works: credit where credit is due
paras: The core insight is simple: if you know the final action was correct, you can work backward and credit the reasoning steps that led there. The agent learns faster because it no longer treats all reasoning paths as equally valid—it learns which intermediate thoughts matter.

Here is the chain of causation. The agent generates multiple possible reasoning trees for the same starting screen. Each tree ends in an action (button press). By checking whether each action matches the correct answer, the paper assigns a simple reward: +1 if correct, 0 or -1 if wrong. The paper then uses a clever averaging rule: an intermediate step is valued as the average of all the steps that followed it. This backward pass ensures that an early reasoning step that appeared in many correct solutions gets a high value, while one that mostly led to wrong actions gets a low value. Finally, the agent is trained using preference learning: when two reasoning paths start identically but diverge, the agent learns to prefer the path that led to a higher-value action. Over multiple rounds, the agent refines its reasoning to favor the paths that work.

stages.s: Screen image, goal, multiple sampled reasoning paths
Check each path's final action against ground truth
Assign reward to each leaf node, high for correct actions
Trace value backward through tree via averaging
Extract preference pairs (high-value vs. low-value reasoning)
Updated agent that prefers high-value reasoning

math.words: value of an intermediate step equals the discount factor times the average value of its child steps
symbols: the value assigned to reasoning step t
discount factor (a number less than 1, typically 0.9 or 0.95)
the number of child steps sampled from step t
the k-th child step following step t

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine step A generates two possible continuations: step B1 and step B2.
Step B1 leads to a correct action (value = 10), step B2 leads to an incorrect action (value = 2).
Step A is assigned value 5.4, which is the weighted average of its children.
If we had a third child C with value 8, then v(A) = 0.9 * (1/3) * (10 + 2 + 8) = 0.9 * 6.67 = 6.0.
The value propagates upward, so early steps in high-value paths are rewarded without manual annotation.

math.note: The discount factor c prevents early steps from being overvalued; averaging ensures that a step is judged by the diversity of outcomes it led to.

charts.title: No preference learning (SFT only)
charts.note: Supervised fine-tuning alone does not teach reasoning quality. The agent memorizes actions.

charts.title: MobileIPL with iterative preference learning
charts.note: Adding preference learning on reasoning steps improves performance on all three benchmarks, even with less training data, because the preference pairs guide the agent toward high-value reasoning patterns rather than just high-value actions, teaching it to reason differently rather than merely memorize.

items.html: If the agent only generates one or two reasoning steps before acting, there is little to score and trace backward. The method works best when agents naturally produce rich, multi-step reasoning.
If the benchmark labels are wrong, the value tracing assigns high value to bad reasoning. The method is only as good as the labeled data.
A reward that only checks the final action right/wrong misses partial credit for reasoning steps that were on the right track but chose a slightly wrong button.
When the agent explores many reasoning paths for each screen, the averaging in value tracing becomes reliable, and the agent learns to consistently choose reasoning that works.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple mobile task: a screen with labeled buttons and a goal (Press the blue button three times, then press Settings). Sample 10 different reasoning paths for each step, where each path generates different intermediate thoughts. Assign a reward to the final action: +1 if correct, 0 if wrong. Trace the values backward using the formula above. Train the agent for two rounds using the preference pairs. The demo should show that after the first round, the agent presses the correct button more often. After the second round, it should reason more like a human, naming the button color or purpose before acting.
demo.metric_eq: Reasoning quality = (correct actions after round 1) minus (correct actions before training), then subtract (actions that reached the goal within 5 steps before training) to confirm the agent is not just lucky
demo.closing: What makes this work: a backward pass through the reasoning tree assigns credit to the steps that worked, without needing a human to annotate each intermediate thought.
